KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry conditions with above normal temperatures
persist through the weekend. This will worsen ongoing water 
resource drought conditions.

KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...
High pressure will build across the region today, then exit to 
the east Sunday. No precipitation is expected through the 
weekend along with above normal temperatures.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Rain is expected Sunday night and Monday 
morning. Enough rain to make a small dent in the drought is 
likely with some places getting over one inch.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
Model trends have stabilized and are mostly settling in a track
of a low pressure system that will bring rain to all of
Northern/Eastern Maine. There is still uncertainty regarding
where the heaviest rain will fall, but we are now pretty
confident in decent rain for all areas, and the uncertainty is
gradually decreasing.

The general consensus is for the low pressure center to track 
northeast roughly along the Downeast coast late Sunday night 
into Monday morning. The low could still track up to about 75 
miles north or south of this best guess track, which will also 
impact where the heaviest rain falls. Just north of the track of
the center of the low pressure, we expect a band of heavy rain 
to set up, with totals up to about 2 inches, all falling within 
about 9 hours. A few thunderstorms are even possible along and 
immediately ahead of the low pressure, most likely near the 
coast. 

For rain totals, we are looking at least 0.5 inch for all areas
except perhaps the extreme NW edge of the state where totals
could be much less. Over 1 inch is expected (90 percent chance)
south of Lincoln, with a 50-85 percent chance of at least 1 
inch from Millinocket north to Madawaska. Totals up to around 2 
inches are possible, with the best chance of a 2 inch total 
south of Lincoln wherever the heaviest banded precipitation sets
up just north of the low pressure track. With it having been so
dry, we do not anticipate impacts other than minor flooding of 
areas with poor drainage.

There is no risk of snow with this system, as the airmass will
be quite mild for this time of year. 

Winds along/north of the low pressure track appear pretty light
through Monday morning, but anywhere south of the low track 
could have some decent south winds. If the low favors a track on
the northern envelope of solutions, some gusts from the south 
to around 40 mph are possible along the coast early Monday.

Models have trended a bit faster with the end time to the rain,
with rain tapering off from west to east probably between 7am 
and 1pm Monday. Colder air starts moving in late Monday 
afternoon, and by dawn Tuesday temperatures will be a bit below 
freezing for most areas. Quite cold from Tuesday into Wednesday.


KEY MESSAGE 3...An active weather pattern is likely from 
Thanksgiving into next weekend. Forecast confidence on any 
particular weather system is low, but travelers should continue
to monitor this period for potential wintry weather.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...
The general weather pattern from Thanksgiving through the 
weekend after Thanksgiving is favorable for active weather. This
is especially important given the active travel period. Looking
through various ensemble model solutions, timing and system 
strength are still quite uncertain. That said, the pattern will
be favorable for Noreasters. 

The first potential Noreaster is late Thanksgiving through 
Friday. There is a bit of a trend in the models toward bringing 
more precipitation with this system, which could include snow. 
That said, there is still a ton of uncertainty in the track and 
strength of the Noreaster. Most models do have a Noreaster of 
some sort tracking NE off the East Coast of the US, but the 
question is if it tracks far enough north/west to bring us 
precipitation, or if it stays out to sea. If the system does 
bring precipitation, it very well could fall as snow, with 
significant wind to accompany it. ECMWF ensembles (physics and 
AI-based) are generally running further north (snowier) with the
track of this system versus the GEFS and GEPS ensembles. GEFS-
AI ensembles are running a fair amount north of the physics-
based GEFS ensembles. To summarize, a bit over half of ensemble 
members have at least a few inches of snow falling somewhere 
over Northern/Eastern Maine late Thanksgiving into Friday. It 
should be noted that some ensemble members also produce 
substantial snow. However, it is still quite early, and there is
still a significant minority that do not bring snow to any part
of Northern/Eastern Maine. 

There is also the potential of another storm which could bring
rain and/or snow around Sunday/Monday, but we need to get
through the potential Thursday/Friday storm first.

In summary, it is still too early to be overly alarmed or alter
travel plans, but be aware of the potential for active weather
that could impact travel Thanksgiving through Sunday, and 
continue to check back with us
